direction: First full Roman Financial story. Fish option 17. Conversational, personal, reflective, with small dry humor. Avoid guru tone.

segments.label: cold_open
segments.text: In 2022, we came to Canada from Ukraine with two kids. And almost all the money we had went into an old car.

segments.label: old_car_reality
segments.text: Not a dream car. Not the car you put in a thumbnail and pretend life is perfect. Just an old car that could take us to work, to school, to groceries, and hopefully not surprise us too often.

segments.label: housing_wall
segments.text: We were renting. We had left our apartment back home. And then I started looking at houses. Eight hundred thousand dollars. Nine hundred thousand. Sometimes one million. I remember looking at those numbers and thinking, this is not difficult. This is impossible.

segments.label: money_is_system
segments.text: And that feeling matters, because a lot of people talk about money like it is just math. But when you arrive in a new country, money is not only math. Money is language. Rules. Credit history. Tax accounts. Rent. Insurance. A car you need before you even understand what the car really costs.

segments.label: family_pressure
segments.text: And on top of that, you are still building normal life. Kids need stability. Groceries still need to be bought. The rent does not care that you are new here.

segments.label: not_a_flex
segments.text: So this is not a video about how we became rich. We did not. This is not a video about which stock you should buy, or which ETF is perfect, or whether you should buy a house tomorrow. This is a personal story about how we went from zero down payment to having options.

segments.label: options_map
segments.text: And honestly, options are underrated. Because when you have no options, every price looks like a wall. When you start building capital, even slowly, the same world begins to look like a map.

segments.label: beginner_again
segments.text: Back in Ukraine, we had never really invested. About a year before moving, I had only a couple thousand dollars to experiment with. That was it. No deep experience. No magic strategy. No secret rich uncle explaining compound interest over dinner.

segments.label: research_late
segments.text: So when we arrived in Canada, I started researching like someone who was already late. I wanted to understand the system. Not perfectly. Just enough to stop feeling completely blind.

segments.label: questions
segments.text: What is a broker? What account should I open? What is the difference between saving and investing? Why does everyone talk about taxes? Why does credit score suddenly matter so much? What is employer matching? What is cashback? Why does every bank have three products that sound almost the same?

segments.label: behind_feeling
segments.text: It was a lot. And at the beginning, the more I learned, the more behind I felt. That is one of the strange parts of immigration. You can be a capable adult, but the financial system can make you feel like a beginner again.

segments.label: enough_to_start
segments.text: But eventually, I found a useful idea. You do not need to understand everything to start. You need to understand enough to start safely.

segments.label: etf_basket
segments.text: For investing, one of those beginner-friendly tools was ETFs. An ETF is basically a basket. Instead of trying to pick one perfect company, you can buy a basket that owns many companies inside it. That does not mean it is risk free. It is still investing. The value can go down. But the idea is simple enough for a beginner to understand.

segments.label: two_paths
segments.text: And simple matters when your life is already full. I personally became interested in investing. I liked reading about companies. So for my own accounts, I bought individual stocks. My wife did not want to do that. And that is completely reasonable. Not everyone wants to spend their evenings reading earnings reports. Some people have healthier hobbies. Apparently.

segments.label: wife_etf_path
segments.text: So for her accounts, I chose the simpler ETF-style path. Baskets instead of stock picking. Same family goal. Different level of complexity. That became one of the first lessons for us: the best system is not the most impressive system. The best system is the one the person can actually keep using.

segments.label: weekly_150
segments.text: After rent, insurance, the old car, groceries, kids, phone bills, and all the normal expenses, we did not have some huge amount left over. But we decided to invest one hundred and fifty dollars a week. That was less than I could make in a day.

segments.label: tiny_vs_house
segments.text: And when you compare one hundred and fifty dollars to a house that costs eight hundred thousand, it feels almost ridiculous. Like trying to fight a forest fire with a water bottle. At the beginning, it felt pointless.

segments.label: boring_middle
segments.text: You put money in. The account still looks small. Then the market moves and sometimes it looks even smaller. Nothing dramatic happens. Nobody claps. You still drive the same old car. You still rent. But this is where the boring part becomes important.

segments.label: repetition
segments.text: A lot of financial progress does not feel like progress while it is happening. It feels like repetition. Every week, a small amount. Every month, learning one more thing. Every year, a little more confidence.

segments.label: tools_stack
segments.text: We learned about investment accounts. We learned about brokers. We learned that employer matching can matter. We learned that cashback is not a wealth strategy, but if you are already spending money, you might as well stop leaving small benefits on the table. We learned that credit is not just a score; it affects real options. We learned that taxes are not a topic you can ignore forever.

segments.label: results
segments.text: Four years later, my investment accounts are around fifty eight thousand six hundred dollars. My wife's accounts are around fifty four thousand five hundred dollars. Together, that is about one hundred and thirteen thousand dollars. These numbers are not here to impress anyone. They are here because they changed the question.

segments.label: new_question
segments.text: Recently, we saw a similar house near the one we rent listed for around five hundred twenty seven thousand dollars. And for the first time, the question was not, how could we ever buy a home? The question became, should we buy one now, or keep growing?

segments.label: details_matter
segments.text: Now, there are important details. Having more than twenty percent of a purchase price does not mean buying is automatically the right decision. There are closing costs. Mortgage payments. Maintenance. Interest rates. Taxes. Opportunity cost. Stability for the family also matters. This is why I do not want this channel to be about pretending money decisions are obvious.

segments.label: channel_promise
segments.text: So the lesson from our first four years is not, copy us. The lesson is this. If you are starting from zero in a new country, the first goal is not to look rich. The first goal is to understand the system well enough to build options. That is what this channel is about. Money after immigration. The mistakes. The tools. The accounts. The car decisions. The house decisions. The investing path. Four years ago, we did not even have the question. And that is the change. We went from zero to options.
